conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is supported and not false, citing prospective observational evidence showing that compression-only CPR is associated with increased survival compared to no bystander CPR.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false.** The best directly relevant retrieved evidence is a five-year prospective observational cohort of 4,415 adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Arizona (2005–09), including 2,900 with no bystander CPR and 849 with layperson compression-only CPR. Its authors concluded that compression-only CPR was *associated with increased survival* versus both conventional CPR and no bystander CPR. Thus, the word **“associated”** accurately reflects the study design and result.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668  
https://cardiovascularbusiness.com/topics/clinical/structural-heart-disease/jama-chest-compression-only-cpr-best-approach-bystanders

**Why this is not definitive causal proof:** people who receive CPR may differ systematically from those who do not—for example, arrest may be witnessed, recognized sooner, occur in public, or receive faster EMS/AED response. Although the Arizona study used multivariable analysis, residual confounding remains possible. Randomly assigning bystanders to provide *no* CPR would be unethical, so the direct hands-only-versus-none comparison necessarily relies largely on observational evidence.

Randomized evidence does support that, among suspected witnessed adult arrests, dispatcher-instructed compression-only CPR can be compared with conventional CPR, with 30-day survival as the endpoint. That trial addresses the *type* of CPR, not whether CPR is preferable to none.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0908991

The mechanism and policy rationale are plausible: hands-only CPR may start faster and reduce interruptions in the first minutes of adult out-of-hospital arrest; international guidance recommends dispatcher instructions for compression-only CPR for adults. This should not be generalized to every arrest mechanism (for example, drowning), where breaths may matter more.  
https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380
